notes: Lesson on tectonic plate movement. Hook: Pangaea puzzle. Three types of plate boundaries with diagrams. Geological evidence section. Video of tectonic simulation. Higher-complexity structure (Class B: 20 units, 6 ECUs).

units.label: Title: Plate Tectonics
units.content_summary: Lesson title

units.label: Hook: Wegener and continental drift (text)
units.content_summary: Alfred Wegener (1912) proposed that continents were once joined as Pangaea and slowly drifted apart over millions of years. Evidence: matching coastlines, identical fossils on different continents, similar rock formations across oceans.

units.label: Pangaea reconstruction map (image)
units.content_summary: World map showing modern continents on one side, and Pangaea reconstruction on other side. Matching colour-coded coastlines show how South America fits into Africa. Labels show today's continents in their Pangaea positions.

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: describe the theory of plate tectonics; identify the three types of plate boundaries; explain evidence for continental drift; describe geological features at each boundary type.

units.label: Tectonic plates overview (text)
units.content_summary: Earth's lithosphere is divided into ~15 major tectonic plates that move on the plastic asthenosphere. Movement driven by convection currents in mantle. Average speed: 2-10 cm/year (roughly fingernail growth rate).

units.label: World tectonic plates map (image)
units.content_summary: World map showing all major tectonic plates with names: Pacific, North American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic, South American, Nazca, Caribbean, Philippine, Juan de Fuca, Arabian, Cocos, Scotia. Boundaries marked.

units.label: Boundary Type 1: Divergent (text)
units.content_summary: Divergent boundaries: plates move apart. New oceanic crust forms as magma rises and solidifies. Creates mid-ocean ridges (e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge). On land: rift valleys (e.g. East African Rift). Results in seafloor spreading.

units.label: Divergent boundary diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Cross-section diagram showing two plates moving apart, magma rising in the gap, forming a mid-ocean ridge. Arrows show plate movement direction and magma upwelling. Labels: divergent boundary, mid-ocean ridge, new crust, magma.

units.label: Boundary Type 2: Convergent (text)
units.content_summary: Convergent boundaries: plates move toward each other. Three subtypes: (1) oceanic-continental: oceanic plate subducts → trench + volcanic mountain chain; (2) oceanic-oceanic: subduction → volcanic island arc; (3) continental-continental: collision → mountain range (no subduction).

units.label: Convergent boundary diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Three-panel diagram showing the three convergent subtypes: (1) Cascades/Andes-type with oceanic subduction and volcanoes; (2) island arc with two oceanic plates; (3) Himalayas-type with two continental plates colliding and buckling upward.

units.label: Boundary Type 3: Transform (text)
units.content_summary: Transform boundaries: plates slide horizontally past each other. No crust created or destroyed. Causes earthquakes. Famous example: San Andreas Fault (California) — Pacific plate sliding north past North American plate. ~7cm/year.

units.label: Transform boundary diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Map and cross-section of the San Andreas Fault. Arrows show Pacific plate moving northwest relative to North American plate. Aerial photo inset showing the visible fault line through California landscape.

units.label: Evidence for plate tectonics: fossils and rocks (text)
units.content_summary: Four lines of evidence: (1) matching coastlines; (2) identical fossil species on separate continents (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris); (3) matching rock formations and mountain ranges across oceans; (4) paleomagnetism — symmetric magnetic striping on seafloor records reversals.

units.label: Fossil evidence map (image)
units.content_summary: World map showing identical fossils found on multiple continents: Mesosaurus (South America and Africa), Glossopteris plant (Antarctica, India, Africa, Australia, South America). Confirms Wegener's Pangaea hypothesis.

units.label: Video: tectonic plates simulation (video)
units.content_summary: Animation showing 250 million years of plate movement from Pangaea to present day. Shows formation and splitting of continents in fast-forward. Narrated with timeline markers at key geological events.

units.label: Geological features summary table (image)
units.content_summary: Summary table: Boundary Type | Movement | Features | Examples. Rows: Divergent (apart, ridges/rifts, Mid-Atlantic Ridge), Convergent (together, trenches/mountains/arcs, Himalayas/Mariana Trench), Transform (sliding, earthquakes, San Andreas).

units.label: Real-world connection: volcanoes and earthquakes distribution (text)
units.content_summary: Volcanoes and earthquakes occur predominantly along plate boundaries — the 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific. This geographical pattern is strong evidence for plate tectonics and explains why certain regions (Japan, Chile, western USA) experience frequent seismic activity.

units.label: Ring of Fire map (image)
units.content_summary: World map showing the Ring of Fire — the zone of frequent earthquakes and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean. Red dots mark earthquake epicentres; triangles mark volcanoes. Coincides closely with plate boundaries shown in U006.

units.label: Practice problems (text)
units.content_summary: Five questions: identify boundary type from description; explain why the Himalayas are still growing; predict what would happen at a specified boundary; describe two pieces of evidence for plate tectonics; identify the boundary type responsible for a given earthquake.
